Avian influenza A(H9N2) has circulated globally across avian hosts for nearly six decades following its initial detection in Wisconsin in 1966. Over subsequent decades, the virus has established widespread endemicity in poultry populations across multiple geographic regions, creating persistent agricultural burdens and public health concerns. Beyond domestic avian infections, H9N2 serves as an established reservoir capable of infecting diverse animal hosts and donating internal gene segments to emerging zoonotic influenza strains, including H5N1 and H7N9. In many poultry-dense settings, H9N2 has become the predominant subtype, complicating disease control because conventional inactivated vaccines frequently fail to provide durable protection against divergent field strains. To address these evolutionary challenges, investigators systematically mapped the genetic determinants within the viral surface glycoprotein that enable H9N2 to alter antigenicity, adapt to mammalian cells, and endure thermal stress. The viral hemagglutinin surface glycoprotein mediates host cell entry and represents the primary target of neutralizing antibodies, placing it at the center of antigenic drift and vaccine formulation. Over prolonged circulation, H9N2 hemagglutinin has diversified into major phylogenetic lineages, including Y439, G1, and BJ94, with BJ94 further dividing into more than sixteen antigenically distinct subgroups exhibiting limited cross-reactivity. To resolve the specific mutational patterns driving this diversity, investigators examined 13,984 full-length hemagglutinin coding sequences retrieved from public databases through June 2025. This curated sequence repository encompassed isolates from four primary host groups: 13,014 sequences from domestic avians, 837 from wild birds, 110 from human clinical cases, and 23 from swine. By aligning these coding sequences with multiple sequence alignment algorithms and segregating them by host origin, the researchers established an extensive baseline to evaluate how natural selection operates across different species boundaries. To quantify amino acid variation across the surface glycoprotein, researchers calculated site-specific Shannon entropy values across all 13,984 sequences, establishing an entropy threshold of 0.2 or greater to classify 179 positions as highly variable substitution hotspots. Each identified site harbored at least two distinct amino acid variants, with residues HA66, HA145, and HA168 exhibiting the greatest diversity. Site 168 displayed the highest overall entropy score of 2.63 across fourteen distinct substitutions, followed by site 145 with an entropy value of 1.81. Cross-species correlation analyses revealed that hotspot substitution profiles in avian isolates closely mirrored those in human isolates, yielding a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.99. Conversely, wild bird isolates displayed the lowest similarity to human isolates, registering a Pearson coefficient of 0.77. At residue 145, serine predominated in wild birds while aspartic acid dominated in poultry and humans. At residue 168, serine predominated in wild birds, alanine in poultry, and human isolates harbored both alanine and asparagine variants, underscoring domestic poultry as an essential transitional reservoir. Recognizing that conventional evolutionary surveillance methods suffer from intrinsic constraints, the authors developed a high-resolution experimental strategy to interrogate hotspot variation. Standard phylogenetic monitoring remains strictly retrospective, restricted to mutations already established in circulating isolates, while traditional in vitro selections rely upon spontaneous mutagenesis that samples mutational space unevenly. To overcome these limitations, the research team constructed a focused deep mutational scanning library targeting all 179 entropy-defined hotspot sites. Using quick-change site-directed mutagenesis, investigators introduced degenerate random codons into each hotspot position within the hemagglutinin gene of the reverse-genetics plasmid rgBJ16/13, representing the A/chicken/Beijing/16/2013 strain. Plasmid pools generated from at least five hundred bacterial colonies per site were harvested and pooled. The resulting hemagglutinin plasmid library was cotransfected into HEK-293T cells alongside seven complementary genomic plasmids encoding the internal segments of rgBJ16/13 to rescue viable viral progeny, generating a primary passage-zero stock that was subsequently amplified in Madin-Darby canine kidney cells. The resulting deep mutational scanning virus library was evaluated using barcoded subamplicon sequencing with unique molecular identifiers to accurately quantify substitution frequencies. The reverse genetics procedure successfully rescued viral variants across all 179 targeted hotspot positions. While initial rescue efficiency for 91.6 percent of individual hotspot sites proved lower than that of parental wild-type rgBJ16/13, sites HA150, HA198, and HA264 showed significantly enhanced rescue, with HA198 reaching a 2.7-fold increase over wild type. Following amplification, deep sequencing revealed that 94.4 percent of hotspot positions maintained substitution frequencies below one percent, with site HA181 exhibiting the highest frequency at 5.4 percent, alongside elevated frequencies at HA115 and HA179. Comparing sitewise library frequencies to the Shannon entropy of natural strains revealed no significant correlation (Pearson R = 0.092), confirming that the experimental library captured unexplored mutational space beyond circulating strains. In contrast, initial rescue efficiency positively correlated with final amplified frequency (Pearson R = 0.22), confirming the predictive value of rescue dynamics. To identify which hotspot residues mediate escape from humoral immunity, the investigators subjected the viral library to three consecutive rounds of in vitro selection using chicken vaccine antiserum raised against rgBJ16/13 at an eighty percent neutralizing concentration. Deep sequencing performed after three rounds of immune selection revealed that selective pressure focused almost exclusively on substitutions at amino acid position 164. Parallel selection using wild-type virus carrying arginine at position 164 confirmed this focus, enriching for a glutamine substitution across two out of three independent biological replicates. To validate these findings, the authors engineered individual recombinant viruses carrying specific substitutions at position 164 and conducted plaque reduction neutralization tests. Analysis of area under the curve measurements demonstrated that viruses carrying 164Q, 164H, 164V, or 164L escaped neutralization by 164R antiserum, causing an approximately one- to two-fold reduction in neutralizing efficacy. Lineage comparisons further revealed that position 164 possesses distinctive lineage-specific profiles, with arginine dominating Y439, glutamine dominating G1, and BJ94 maintaining both variants, establishing residue 164 as an essential determinant of antigenic drift. The investigation subsequently examined host-dependent viral replication dynamics by serially passaging the mixed hotspot library through five consecutive rounds in two distinct biological environments: mammalian Madin-Darby canine kidney cells and ten-day-old embryonated chicken eggs. Over the five serial passages, viral titers displayed contrasting trajectories, increasing progressively in canine cell culture while showing a relative decrease during propagation in embryonated eggs. Next-generation sequencing performed on fifth-passage viral populations revealed profound, system-specific alterations in substitution profiles. In mammalian cell culture, an asparagine-to-histidine substitution at residue 115 (N115H) underwent rapid positive selection, expanding from baseline library levels to constitute 54.6 percent of the total viral population by the fifth passage. In marked contrast, passaging within embryonated chicken eggs selected for entirely distinct genetic alterations, leading to the enrichment of an S334G substitution to 73.5 percent abundance alongside an L224R substitution at 19.5 percent frequency, demonstrating that host cellular environments impose divergent selective pressures upon the avian influenza mutational repertoire. Statistical correlation analyses of substitution frequencies further illuminated the structural divergence between the two host-passaged viral populations. The fifth-passage population harvested from mammalian cell culture maintained a strong positive correlation with the original input library, registering a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.84, which indicated that despite the strong enrichment of N115H, broad genetic diversity across other hotspot positions was largely preserved. Conversely, passage through embryonated eggs triggered extensive restructuring of the mutational spectrum, yielding a low Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.14 when compared to the starting library. To confirm whether the dominant mammalian mutation conferred a measurable fitness advantage, researchers assessed multi-cycle replication kinetics in confluent canine kidney cells infected at a multiplicity of infection of 0.005. Growth curve analyses across three independent biological replicates demonstrated that recombinant viruses bearing the N115H substitution attained significantly higher infectious titers than parental wild-type rgBJ16/13 at 12, 24, and 36 hours post-infection, establishing that this hotspot substitution enhances viral replication efficiency in mammalian systems. In addition to host adaptation and immune evasion, the researchers evaluated hemagglutinin environmental stability, an essential physical parameter that influences viral persistence, transmission dynamics, and zoonotic potential. To identify substitutions increasing structural resilience, the 179-pool hotspot library was subjected to thermal selection at 52.5 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes, an exposure that inactivates over 90 percent of wild-type rgBJ16/13. Normalized plaque assays revealed that substitution pools at positions 14, 134, 218, 302, and 436 conferred markedly enhanced heat tolerance. Deep sequencing of eleven heat-selected sites—positions 4, 13, 14, 40, 134, 176, 218, 230, 302, 306, and 436—demonstrated a drastic reduction in sequence entropy, yielding single, heat-resistant amino acids. To validate these thermal phenotypes, authors tested purified viral variants carrying I134L and L230S within the receptor-binding domain and V306L within the stem region. Inactivation assays across a temperature gradient from 50 to 55 degrees Celsius confirmed that all three substitutions consistently increased heat resistance relative to wild-type virus. By linking computational entropy calculations derived from natural sequence databases directly to high-throughput experimental mutagenesis and phenotypic selection, this research establishes an integrated functional map of avian influenza hemagglutinin evolvability. The authors noted that whereas residue 164 exhibits extensive polymorphism among circulating H9N2 viruses, this identical position remains strictly conserved across other avian influenza subtypes such as H5 and H7, illustrating why reliance on passive sequence monitoring alone fails to anticipate emerging evolutionary trajectories. Furthermore, the exclusion of conserved epitopes from the library ensured that experimental screening focused specifically on regions possessing genuine adaptive plasticity rather than structural fragility. These findings demonstrate that H9N2 antigenic diversity, cross-species replication competence, and environmental stability are orchestrated by a discrete set of mutable hotspots that can be systematically identified and functionally characterized prior to their widespread emergence in nature. Consequently, the authors conclude that this high-throughput deep mutational scanning framework provides an essential scientific platform for predictive viral risk assessment, proactive molecular surveillance of field strains, and the rational engineering of stabilized, broadly protective next-generation poultry vaccines. Thursday, November 12, 2026 Referral (NEJM): Autoantibodies against Type I Interferons and Death from H7N7 Avian Influenza AutoAb development in population credit Human autoantibodies against type I interferons in severe viral disease #19,413 We've a fascinating correspondence - published yesterday (Nov 11th) in the NEJM - which links a relatively rare autoimmune dysfunction (autoantibodies against Type I Interferons) to increased severity of novel flu infection. The authors hypothesize that those with this condition could potentially act as “patients zero” in emerging viral pandemics. Since this correspondence is not open access, I'm only able to give some background and a brief synopsis. Those already familiar with the events of the 2003 H7N7 outbreak, and the recent discoveries surrounding this autoimmune condition, may prefer to proceed directly to the link below. Autoantibodies against Type I Interferons and Death from H7N7 Avian Influenza Published November 11, 2026 N Engl J Med 2026;395:1963-1965 DOI: 10.1056/NEJMc2608446 VOL. 395 NO. 19 Copyright © 2026 For those preferring a review: In 2003, the Netherlands saw an outbreak of H7N7 that resulted in the loss of 30 million birds across 1,000 farms, and saw scores of mild human infections and the death of a veterinarian (see Eurosurveillance Human-to-human transmission of avian influenza A/H7N7, The Netherlands, 2003). Another analysis, performed by the RIVM (Ministry of Health) found the spread of the virus to be much greater than originally reported, citing as many as 1,000 human infections (see Executive summary Avian Flu Epidemic 2003: Public health consequences). Both reports cited likely human-to-human transmission, with the RIVM study finding ` . . 58.9% of the family contacts of persons having direct exposure to poultry had a measurable response in the HI test.' Most of these cases reported mild symptoms; primarily conjunctivitis. A minority reported mild-or-moderate flu-like symptoms (often in conjunction with conjunctivitis), and one patient died. While nowhere as deadly to humans as H5N1 or H7N9, this H7N7 outbreak serves as a cautionary tale on the susceptibility of humans to novel influenza. It also raises questions about the wide spectrum of outcomes from novel flu infection. Relatively recently a rare immune dysfunction - autoantibodies against type I interferons - has been tagged as a likely determinant of severity in viral infections. Six months ago, a review article in Current Opinion in Virology (Human autoantibodies against type I interferons in severe viral disease by Groen & Hale) reported: Highlights AutoAb development is influenced by age, genetics, immune tolerance, and infections. IFN-I autoAbs heighten risk for severe infections and live-vaccine adverse events. Targeted diagnostic screening for IFN-I autoAbs could benefit certain individuals. Understanding autoAb mechanisms will help devise potential therapeutic strategies. While first discovered in the early 1980s, it wasn't until COVID that AutoAbs impact on viral infections was really appreciated (see Nature Human genetic and immunological determinants of critical COVID-19 pneumonia). All of which brings us to the NEJM correspondence, where the authors went back and tested stored serum from 35 patients from the 2003 H7N7 outbreak, including the 58 y.o. veterinarian who died. They found the fatal case had autoantibodies neutralizing interferon-α, -ω, and -β, while 2 of the remaining 34 mild cases had autoantibodies neutralizing interferon-β only. Since antibodies against all three subtypes are rare in people under 60, the authors say this is unlikely to be by chance. Strengthening their case, the fatal H5N1 case in Louisiana in early 2025 carried IFN-I autoAbs. Autoantibodies neutralizing type I IFNs in a fatal case of H5N1 avian influenza Qian Zhang Corresponding Author , Taylor S. Conrad , Marcela Moncada-Velez , Kaijun Jiang ,Anastasija Cupic , Jonathan Eaton , Kimberley Hutchinson ,Adrian Gervais ,Ruyue Chen , Anne Puel , Paul Bastard , Aurelie Cobat ,Thersa Sokol , RyanA. Langlois ,Lisa Miorin , Adolfo García-Sastre ,John A. Vanchiere , Jean-Laurent Casanova Corresponding Author Author and Article Information J Exp Med (2026) 223 (3): e20251962. https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20251962 While it is well established that avian flu viruses have a hard time establishing themselves in humans, and that human-to-human transmission is uncommon, this rare autoimmune condition could provide a foothold for novel viruses like H5N1, H7N7, and H9N2 to adapt to humans. At least that's the theory. Admittedly, one based on limited evidence. But if it turns out to be correct, it becomes even more imperative that we take steps to prevent spillovers (PPEs, seasonal flu vaccines to prevent coinfection and reassortment, etc.), and to treat even mild cases as potential public health threats. Policies which, based on recent anecdotal reports (see Newsweek Farm Workers Sound Alarm on Underreported Bird Flu Numbers), still appear to be lacking. Wednesday, November 11, 2026 UK Scotland: H5N5 Reported In Eurasian Otters - AIPZs Declared for England and Scotland #19,412 We've been watching the co-circulation and spread of an H5N5 subtype of avian flu - primarily in the high latitude regions of the Northern Hemisphere - for the past 3 years (see Preprint: H5N5 virus transmission is driven by repeated cross-Atlantic introductions and transmission among high latitude seabirds). We've seen numerous reports of H5N5 from Norway, Svalbard island, Iceland, and eastern Canada, often infecting mammals, including cats, polar bears, raccoons, foxes, and walruses. In the spring of 2025, the UK reported 15 grey seals infected with H5N5. The following November, in UK: HPAI H5N5 Rising, we saw a sudden shift in H5N5 activity in wild birds in the UK, with the APHA reporting: Since our previous outbreak assessment on 7 October 2024, there have been no new reports of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) H5 clade 2.3.3.4b in domestic poultry in Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales). There have, however, been 15 more HPAI H5 clade 2.3.3.4b events involving 26 “found-dead” wild birds in Great Britain. Of these, 25 were HPAI H5N5 with 1 case of HPAI H5N1. Also in November of 2025 the United States reported the first (and fatal) human infection with H5N5. While still a minor player in the global scheme of things, H5N5 continues to show surprising resilience and spread. While most of these reports have involved wild birds and/or small mammals, in early October Scotland reported an outbreak of H5N5 in commercial poultry in Ness, Isle of Lewis. 3 October 2026 Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N5 was confirmed in commercial backyard poultry in Ness, Isle of Lewis, Scotland (AIV 2026/20). A 3km protection zone and 10km surveillance zone has been declared around the premises. This is the first outbreak of the 2026 to 2027 season and following confirmation of this case, GB has lost its freedom from highly pathogenic avian influenza (bird flu) status. In an update, posted today by defra, the UK government has announced AIPZs (avian influenza protection zones) have been declared for both England and Scotland. 11 November 2026 AIPZ declared in England and Scotland from 11 November 2026 Following a number of findings of highly pathogenic avian influenza in wild birds and detections in poultry and increased risk levels, an avian influenza prevention zone (AIPZ) has been declared covering England and Scotland to mitigate the risk of further outbreaks of disease occurring. This means that it is a legal requirement for all bird keepers in England and Scotland to follow strict biosecurity to prevent bird flu and stop it spreading. You can read more information on the requirements for certain types of bird: in the declaration for the AIPZ in England In the declaration for the AIPZ in Scotland Additionally, today defra has updated their avian flu in on-avian wildlife list for the first time since early March, adding three recent H5N5 detections over 5 weeks. The most recent High pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) in Great Britain and Europe Update Assessment (#11) - dated Nov. 6th, but released yesterday- carries the following map showing 81 detections of HPAI H5 since Oct 1st. I've circled the H5N5 detections. For now, all are on the western and northern coastlines, which fits the narrative that it is primarily carried by sea and shore birds. Whether it can establish itself further inland remains to be seen. But for now, it seems to be holding its own against H5N1. EID Journal: Cross-Protection against Influenza A(H5) Clade 2.3.4.4b Viruses after A(H1N1)pdm09 Infection #19,411 Over the past 32 months we've seen at least six dozen human infections from HPAI H5 (H5N1 & H5N5) in the United States, and while most have been described as mild or moderate, 3 people have died. It seems likely, based on limited seroprevalence testing (see JAMA Open: Asymptomatic Human Infections With Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Confirmed by Molecular and Serologic Testing), that the actual number of infections is higher. Which suggests that H5N1 may not be quite as deadly as originally feared. Of course, even a 2%-3% fatality rate would put it in the same league as the 1918 pandemic. An early assessment by the CDC (July 14th, 2024 H5N1 Update) reported that `. . . that there is extremely low to no population immunity to clade 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1) viruses in the United States'. Since then, however, we've seen a number of studies which have reported serological evidence of limited immunity - particularly in older cohorts - against some strains of H5N1. Probably not enough to prevent infection, but perhaps enough to reduce the severity of infection. Initially, the focus was on HA immune imprinting (see Nature: Declan Butler On How Your First Bout Of Flu Leaves A Lasting Impression), where the HA group (1 or 2) you are first exposed to is thought to provide some degree of protection against other HAs in that group. How much real-world protection early or past H1/H2 exposure might offer against H5Nx - or how long it might last - are unknown, but it has been suggested it might provide an `edge' against severe disease. More recently, we've seen attempts to quantify the impact of the first NA (Neuraminidase) one is exposed to (see last December's Nature Comms: Pre-existing Cross-reactive Immunity to HPAI 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1) Virus in the United States). This study found`very low levels of pre-existing binding antibodies to the HA head of the HPAI A(H5N1) 2.3.4.4b virus', but slightly more encouragingly, `. . . substantial cross-reactive binding antibodies to N1 neuraminidase (NA) of 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1). Regarding the the value of cross-reactive antibodies to the N1 Neuraminidase, the authors wrote: Neuraminidase antibodies have been considered as an independent correlate to protect against influenza 20. Although they cannot prevent infection, neuraminidase antibodies can prevent virus egress, reduce viral shedding, and thus could attenuate disease and lessen disease severity 21,22,23. All of which brings us to a new research letter, published yesterday in the EID Journal, which reports that ferrets pre-exposed to H1N1 saw less severe illness when challenged with H5N1 or H5N5 than influenza-naive ferrets. A few caveats: While an encouraging finding, this was a relatively small study, and ferrets aren't a perfect analog for humans. Also, pre-exposed ferrets only had one prior exposure - to H1N1pdm09 - whereas the human population typically has a much messier exposure history to a variety of flu viruses (many first imprinted with H3N2, or pre-2009 H1N1). The challenge experiments appear to have been conducted roughly 3 months after H1N1 infection, and it is unknown if - or how quickly - protection might wane. Not unexpectedly, pre-exposed ferrets exposed to H5N5 did not fare quite as well as those challenged with H5N1, and there are no guarantees that any future H5 pandemic would carry a closely matching N1 Neuraminidase. Still, this is a fascinating report, and it may partially explain why recent H5N1 infections have been less deadly than originally feared. Follow the link to read the report in its entirety. Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Research Letter Cross-Protection against Influenza A(H5) Clade 2.3.4.4b Viruses after A(H1N1)pdm09 Infection Xiangjie Sun, Jessica A. Belser, Zhu-Nan Li, Nicole Brock, Joanna A. Pulit-Penaloza, Troy J. Kieran, Claudia Pappas, Hui Zeng, Jessie C. Chang, Paul J. Carney, Brandon L. Bradley-Ferrell, James Stevens, Min Z. Levine, and Taronna R. Maines Abstract We challenged ferrets previously infected with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus with H5N1 or H5N5 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses to assess cross-protection. Results show that previous A(H1N1)pdm09 virus immunity conferred partial protection against both viruses, with slightly reduced protection against H5N5 compared with H5N1, potentially reflecting the absence of cross-reactive N5 neuraminidase antibodies. (SNIP) Preimmune ferrets challenged with either H5N1 or H5N5 virus shed similar levels of virus in nasal wash samples during days 1–4 postinfection (range of mean peak titers 103.8–105.2 PFU/mL) as naive controls but exhibited reduced titers in throat swab samples on day 4 for H5N5 virus and days 2 and 3 for H5N1 virus (Figure 2, panels A, B). Viral clearance from nasal washes occurred 2–4 days earlier in preimmune ferrets. We detected H5N1 virus less frequently in rectal swab samples from preimmune animals than from naive controls, whereas we did not observe that reduction for ferrets infected with H5N5 virus (Figure 2, panels A, B). Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus preimmunity did not substantially reduce viral titers in the upper respiratory tract (nasal turbinates) or soft palate after H5N1 or H5N5 virus challenge (Figure 2, panels C, D). However, A(H1N1)pdm09 preimmunity largely prevented viral dissemination to the lower respiratory tract (trachea and lungs) and extrapulmonary tissues for both viruses, with only sporadic low-level viral detection. However, intestinal viral titers were comparable between preimmune and naive ferrets challenged with H5N5 virus (Figure 2, panels C, D). Detection of group 1 HA stalk antibodies after A(H1N1)pdm09 infection (Appendix Figure), together with previous evidence of HA stalk-mediated cross-protection against disease caused by the influenza A viruses within the same phylogenetic group (3,9), suggests that cross-reactive HA stalk antibodies might contribute to protection against A(H5) viruses. In addition, N1 cross-reactivity might further enhance protection against H5N1 virus. Consistent with our findings, limited N5 cross-reactivity has been reported in humans despite detectable N1 responses (10). Further studies using H5-specific HA stalk antigens and functional assays are needed to determine the contribution of cross-reactive antibodies and cellular immunity to protection against zoonotic influenza A viruses. Our findings showed that previous A(H1N1)pdm09 viral infection conferred partial cross-protection against H5N1 and H5N5 viruses in ferrets, reducing disease severity, lethality, and viral dissemination. Dr. Sun is a microbiologist in the Influenza Division, National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Atlanta, Georgia, USA. Her research primarily focuses on using the ferret model to understand influenza virus pathogenicity and transmissibility. Oregon ODA Reports Its First Outbreak of HPAI H5 In Dairy Cattle #19,410 A little over a month ago Washington State became the 20th U.S. state to report HPAI H5N1 in dairy cattle, and since has racked up 43 outbreaks. Just over a week ago (Nov 2nd), Indiana Reported their 1st Infected Herds (n=2) becoming the 21st affected state, and late yesterday Oregon became the 22nd. Oregon had previously reported two pigs infected with H5N1 in the fall of 2024 on a mixed species farm which had experienced an outbreak in poultry. Oregon has also reported 62 poultry outbreaks, primarily among backyard producers (including 1 human infection). With the recent addition of Washington and Oregon, only Montana and North Dakota remain unscathed in the western half of the nation. Thursday, November 12, 2026 Referral (NEJM): Autoantibodies against Type I Interferons and Death from H7N7 Avian Influenza AutoAb development in population credit Human autoantibodies against type I interferons in severe viral disease #19,413 We've a fascinating correspondence - published yesterday (Nov 11th) in the NEJM - which links a relatively rare autoimmune dysfunction (autoantibodies against Type I Interferons) to increased severity of novel flu infection. The authors hypothesize that those with this condition could potentially act as “patients zero” in emerging viral pandemics. Since this correspondence is not open access, I'm only able to give some background and a brief synopsis. Those already familiar with the events of the 2003 H7N7 outbreak, and the recent discoveries surrounding this autoimmune condition, may prefer to proceed directly to the link below. Autoantibodies against Type I Interferons and Death from H7N7 Avian Influenza Published November 11, 2026 N Engl J Med 2026;395:1963-1965 DOI: 10.1056/NEJMc2608446 VOL. 395 NO. 19 Copyright © 2026 For those preferring a review: In 2003, the Netherlands saw an outbreak of H7N7 that resulted in the loss of 30 million birds across 1,000 farms, and saw scores of mild human infections and the death of a veterinarian (see Eurosurveillance Human-to-human transmission of avian influenza A/H7N7, The Netherlands, 2003). Another analysis, performed by the RIVM (Ministry of Health) found the spread of the virus to be much greater than originally reported, citing as many as 1,000 human infections (see Executive summary Avian Flu Epidemic 2003: Public health consequences). Both reports cited likely human-to-human transmission, with the RIVM study finding ` . . 58.9% of the family contacts of persons having direct exposure to poultry had a measurable response in the HI test.' Most of these cases reported mild symptoms; primarily conjunctivitis. A minority reported mild-or-moderate flu-like symptoms (often in conjunction with conjunctivitis), and one patient died. While nowhere as deadly to humans as H5N1 or H7N9, this H7N7 outbreak serves as a cautionary tale on the susceptibility of humans to novel influenza. It also raises questions about the wide spectrum of outcomes from novel flu infection. Relatively recently a rare immune dysfunction - autoantibodies against type I interferons - has been tagged as a likely determinant of severity in viral infections. Six months ago, a review article in Current Opinion in Virology (Human autoantibodies against type I interferons in severe viral disease by Groen & Hale) reported: Highlights AutoAb development is influenced by age, genetics, immune tolerance, and infections. IFN-I autoAbs heighten risk for severe infections and live-vaccine adverse events. Targeted diagnostic screening for IFN-I autoAbs could benefit certain individuals. Understanding autoAb mechanisms will help devise potential therapeutic strategies. While first discovered in the early 1980s, it wasn't until COVID that AutoAbs impact on viral infections was really appreciated (see Nature Human genetic and immunological determinants of critical COVID-19 pneumonia). All of which brings us to the NEJM correspondence, where the authors went back and tested stored serum from 35 patients from the 2003 H7N7 outbreak, including the 58 y.o. veterinarian who died. They found the fatal case had autoantibodies neutralizing interferon-α, -ω, and -β, while 2 of the remaining 34 mild cases had autoantibodies neutralizing interferon-β only. Since antibodies against all three subtypes are rare in people under 60, the authors say this is unlikely to be by chance. Strengthening their case, the fatal H5N1 case in Louisiana in early 2025 carried IFN-I autoAbs. Langlois ,Lisa Miorin , Adolfo García-Sastre ,John A. Vanchiere , Jean-Laurent Casanova Corresponding Author Author and Article Information J Exp Med (2026) 223 (3): e20251962. https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20251962 While it is well established that avian flu viruses have a hard time establishing themselves in humans, and that human-to-human transmission is uncommon, this rare autoimmune condition could provide a foothold for novel viruses like H5N1, H7N7, and H9N2 to adapt to humans. At least that's the theory. Admittedly, one based on limited evidence. But if it turns out to be correct, it becomes even more imperative that we take steps to prevent spillovers (PPEs, seasonal flu vaccines to prevent coinfection and reassortment, etc.), and to treat even mild cases as potential public health threats. Policies which, based on recent anecdotal reports (see Newsweek Farm Workers Sound Alarm on Underreported Bird Flu Numbers), still appear to be lacking. Wednesday, November 11, 2026 UK Scotland: H5N5 Reported In Eurasian Otters - AIPZs Declared for England and Scotland #19,412 We've been watching the co-circulation and spread of an H5N5 subtype of avian flu - primarily in the high latitude regions of the Northern Hemisphere - for the past 3 years (see Preprint: H5N5 virus transmission is driven by repeated cross-Atlantic introductions and transmission among high latitude seabirds). We've seen numerous reports of H5N5 from Norway, Svalbard island, Iceland, and eastern Canada, often infecting mammals, including cats, polar bears, raccoons, foxes, and walruses. In the spring of 2025, the UK reported 15 grey seals infected with H5N5. The following November, in UK: HPAI H5N5 Rising, we saw a sudden shift in H5N5 activity in wild birds in the UK, with the APHA reporting: Since our previous outbreak assessment on 7 October 2024, there have been no new reports of high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) H5 clade 2.3.3.4b in domestic poultry in Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales). There have, however, been 15 more HPAI H5 clade 2.3.3.4b events involving 26 “found-dead” wild birds in Great Britain. Of these, 25 were HPAI H5N5 with 1 case of HPAI H5N1. Also in November of 2025 the United States reported the first (and fatal) human infection with H5N5. While still a minor player in the global scheme of things, H5N5 continues to show surprising resilience and spread. While most of these reports have involved wild birds and/or small mammals, in early October Scotland reported an outbreak of H5N5 in commercial poultry in Ness, Isle of Lewis. 3 October 2026 Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N5 was confirmed in commercial backyard poultry in Ness, Isle of Lewis, Scotland (AIV 2026/20). A 3km protection zone and 10km surveillance zone has been declared around the premises. This is the first outbreak of the 2026 to 2027 season and following confirmation of this case, GB has lost its freedom from highly pathogenic avian influenza (bird flu) status. In an update, posted today by defra, the UK government has announced AIPZs (avian influenza protection zones) have been declared for both England and Scotland. 11 November 2026 AIPZ declared in England and Scotland from 11 November 2026 Following a number of findings of highly pathogenic avian influenza in wild birds and detections in poultry and increased risk levels, an avian influenza prevention zone (AIPZ) has been declared covering England and Scotland to mitigate the risk of further outbreaks of disease occurring. This means that it is a legal requirement for all bird keepers in England and Scotland to follow strict biosecurity to prevent bird flu and stop it spreading. You can read more information on the requirements for certain types of bird: in the declaration for the AIPZ in England In the declaration for the AIPZ in Scotland Additionally, today defra has updated their avian flu in on-avian wildlife list for the first time since early March, adding three recent H5N5 detections over 5 weeks. The most recent High pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) in Great Britain and Europe Update Assessment (#11) - dated Nov. 6th, but released yesterday- carries the following map showing 81 detections of HPAI H5 since Oct 1st. I've circled the H5N5 detections. For now, all are on the western and northern coastlines, which fits the narrative that it is primarily carried by sea and shore birds. Whether it can establish itself further inland remains to be seen. But for now, it seems to be holding its own against H5N1. EID Journal: Cross-Protection against Influenza A(H5) Clade 2.3.4.4b Viruses after A(H1N1)pdm09 Infection #19,411 Over the past 32 months we've seen at least six dozen human infections from HPAI H5 (H5N1 & H5N5) in the United States, and while most have been described as mild or moderate, 3 people have died. It seems likely, based on limited seroprevalence testing (see JAMA Open: Asymptomatic Human Infections With Avian Influenza A(H5N1) Virus Confirmed by Molecular and Serologic Testing), that the actual number of infections is higher. Which suggests that H5N1 may not be quite as deadly as originally feared. Of course, even a 2%-3% fatality rate would put it in the same league as the 1918 pandemic. An early assessment by the CDC (July 14th, 2024 H5N1 Update) reported that `. . . that there is extremely low to no population immunity to clade 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1) viruses in the United States'. Since then, however, we've seen a number of studies which have reported serological evidence of limited immunity - particularly in older cohorts - against some strains of H5N1. Probably not enough to prevent infection, but perhaps enough to reduce the severity of infection. Initially, the focus was on HA immune imprinting (see Nature: Declan Butler On How Your First Bout Of Flu Leaves A Lasting Impression), where the HA group (1 or 2) you are first exposed to is thought to provide some degree of protection against other HAs in that group. How much real-world protection early or past H1/H2 exposure might offer against H5Nx - or how long it might last - are unknown, but it has been suggested it might provide an `edge' against severe disease. More recently, we've seen attempts to quantify the impact of the first NA (Neuraminidase) one is exposed to (see last December's Nature Comms: Pre-existing Cross-reactive Immunity to HPAI 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1) Virus in the United States). This study found`very low levels of pre-existing binding antibodies to the HA head of the HPAI A(H5N1) 2.3.4.4b virus', but slightly more encouragingly, `. . . substantial cross-reactive binding antibodies to N1 neuraminidase (NA) of 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1). Regarding the the value of cross-reactive antibodies to the N1 Neuraminidase, the authors wrote: Neuraminidase antibodies have been considered as an independent correlate to protect against influenza 20. Although they cannot prevent infection, neuraminidase antibodies can prevent virus egress, reduce viral shedding, and thus could attenuate disease and lessen disease severity 21,22,23. All of which brings us to a new research letter, published yesterday in the EID Journal, which reports that ferrets pre-exposed to H1N1 saw less severe illness when challenged with H5N1 or H5N5 than influenza-naive ferrets. A few caveats: While an encouraging finding, this was a relatively small study, and ferrets aren't a perfect analog for humans. Also, pre-exposed ferrets only had one prior exposure - to H1N1pdm09 - whereas the human population typically has a much messier exposure history to a variety of flu viruses (many first imprinted with H3N2, or pre-2009 H1N1). The challenge experiments appear to have been conducted roughly 3 months after H1N1 infection, and it is unknown if - or how quickly - protection might wane. Not unexpectedly, pre-exposed ferrets exposed to H5N5 did not fare quite as well as those challenged with H5N1, and there are no guarantees that any future H5 pandemic would carry a closely matching N1 Neuraminidase. Still, this is a fascinating report, and it may partially explain why recent H5N1 infections have been less deadly than originally feared. Follow the link to read the report in its entirety. Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Research Letter Cross-Protection against Influenza A(H5) Clade 2.3.4.4b Viruses after A(H1N1)pdm09 Infection Xiangjie Sun, Jessica A. Belser, Zhu-Nan Li, Nicole Brock, Joanna A. Pulit-Penaloza, Troy J. Kieran, Claudia Pappas, Hui Zeng, Jessie C. Chang, Paul J. Carney, Brandon L. Bradley-Ferrell, James Stevens, Min Z. Levine, and Taronna R. Maines Abstract We challenged ferrets previously infected with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus with H5N1 or H5N5 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses to assess cross-protection. Results show that previous A(H1N1)pdm09 virus immunity conferred partial protection against both viruses, with slightly reduced protection against H5N5 compared with H5N1, potentially reflecting the absence of cross-reactive N5 neuraminidase antibodies. Photograph: Jim Holden/Alamy Bird flu fears prompt orders for farmers to keep poultry inside in England and Scotland Increased risk of devastating strain means restrictions imposed for second year in a row on those keeping birds Poultry and captive birds across England and Scotland must be kept inside for the second year in a row due to an increased risk of a devastating strain of bird flu. The British government has issued an England-wide avian influenza prevention zone, meaning individuals with 50 or more poultry or captive birds must house them inside. A similar designation was made across the whole of Scotland on Tuesday. Birdkeepers must also follow enhanced biosecurity measures including reporting changes in egg production and reporting suspected disease immediately to the Animal and Plant Health Agency. The government said the declaration followed an increased risk and escalating number of confirmations of the highly pathogenic avian influenza, or bird flu, in kept and wild birds. A prevention zone was also declared across all of England, Scotland and Wales in 2025. The disease has been spreading rapidly since 2014 and has devastated UK wild bird populations since the summer of 2021. It has also spread across an unusually broad range of species around the world, including in four of the five main southern elephant seal populations. In some south Atlantic colonies, more than 90% of newborn pups have died, alongside about half of all adult females. Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow? Read more The disease has also been detected in humans, with 11 deaths recorded globally between 1 January and 4 August 2025. This strain of bird flu causes illness and high death rates in birds, and flu-like symptoms and conjunctivitis in humans who come into close contact with infected animals. The British government said the current risk to human health from bird flu remained very low. The government says it does not anticipate an impact on the availability of Christmas turkeys or other seasonal poultry for consumers. The Food Safety Authority said properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, were safe to eat. The UK chief veterinary officer, Christine Middlemiss, said: “Having avian influenza confirmed in your flock can be devastating. An ODFW release said the majority of these reports currently are from the Willamette Valley and the Cackling goose – a smaller subspecies of the Canada goose – appears to be the most heavily affected. IdentifyPlants Discover more Shop Bird Supplies Book a Safari Check Symptoms ODFW urges people to avoid contact with sick birds and keep pets away. Dead birds can be disposed of – it is recommended to wear disposable gloves and a mask, and double-bag the carcass before putting it in the trash. There is no effective treatment for HPAI-infected wild and domestic birds, and the virus can spread rapidly among bird populations and potentially to other wildlife. That means that sick birds cannot go to a wildlife rehabilitation center and should not be captured live by the public. IdentifyPlants Typical symptoms in wild waterfowl include lethargy, inability to fly, erratic behavior, loss of coordination, cloudy eyes, swimming in circles, and head shaking. However, some dabbling ducks may carry the virus without symptoms, spreading it through their feces to other birds and wetlands. Birds usually die within 72 hours of showing clinical signs. Infected wild mammals may appear sick or neurologically abnormal, or be found dead after consuming infected birds, and should also be reported. Those who see dead or sick domestic birds should immediately call the Oregon Department of Agriculture by calling 503-986-4711 or 800-347-7028. WhatsAppLinkedInTwitterFacebookEmailShare By MBN Staff MBN staff Thu, 11/12/2026 16:22 3 min read DIA READ ARTICLE Ready to read 0:00 1x In this week’s Mexican agribusiness and food news, federal sanitary authorities executed emergency containment measures in Yucatán following Mexico’s first commercial H5N1 avian influenza outbreak since 2024, while Nestlé doubled its industrial investment commitment in Mexico to US$2 billion by 2030. Meanwhile, Michoacán resumed avocado exports following a 10-day grower strike over farmgate prices and digital traceability rules, flour millers navigated domestic white corn purchase mandates, and boxed beef exports surged to the United States alongside expanding Asian meat trade. Harvest the insights! This is your Week in Agribusiness & Food! H5N1 Outbreak in Yucatan Puts Poultry Sector on High Alert Federal sanitary agency SENASICA and its Central Commission for Animal Health (CPA) established a 10km quarantine perimeter and depopulated nearly 225,000 birds on a commercial laying-hen farm in Umán, Yucatán, after confirming Mexico’s first commercial H5N1 avian influenza outbreak since May 2024. The biosecurity alert has prompted major poultry integrators—including Industrias Bachoco and Pilgrim's Pride México—to tighten disease surveillance and contingency distribution plans amid tight table egg supply chains. Nestlé Doubles Mexico Investment to US$2 Billion by 2030 Following executive meetings with President Claudia Sheinbaum at the National Palace, Nestlé announced it will double its industrial capital investment in Mexico to US$2 billion through 2030, distinct from its separate US$2 billion agricultural procurement forecast. The capital deployment will expand manufacturing plants in Toluca and Cuautitlán, build a 90,000-pallet distribution center in Zumpango, and integrate 2,000 Veracruz coffee producers to strengthen domestic robusta sourcing and supply chain resilience. Michoacan Avocado Shipments Resume Following 10-Day Halt Avocado harvesting and export operations in Michoacán resumed after a 10-day strike by Productores Unidos de Aguacate over depressed farmgate prices and administrative friction surrounding the state’s VELAGRO digital tracking platform. Negotiations clarified that smallholders with five hectares or less are exempt from direct IMSS employer registration and that export labor certificates rest primarily with commercial exporters, easing acute cold-storage bottlenecks for US importers. How Mexican Flour Millers Balance Domestic and Imported Corn Under SADER’s White Corn Production and Commercialization System, major nixtamalized flour producers—including GRUMA and Minsa—are prioritizing forward purchase agreements with domestic farmers before turning to US imports. While forward contracts stabilize grain availability, millers face margin compression from rising energy and transport costs, capped tortilla prices under the National Corn-Tortilla Agreement, and new antitrust rules eliminating exclusivity clauses with tortilla shops. What It Takes for Mexican Pork and Beef to Enter Asia Backed by its top-tier animal health status from the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and 149 export-certified Federal Inspection Type (TIF) plants, Mexico is expanding pork and beef shipments across Asia. Following Kekén’s inaugural pork shipment to the Philippines in late October, exporters are leveraging inspection equivalence in Japan and bilateral food safety agreements with South Korea to diversify protein trade beyond North America. Mexican Beef Exports to the US: How Fast and Who Leads? With US border restrictions on live cattle due to the screwworm outbreak cutting live calf shipments by 80%, Mexican producers are fattening and slaughtering cattle domestically, propelling boxed beef exports toward an estimated 400,000 tons in 2026. Led by SuKarne—which accounts for roughly 75% of national beef exports—and bolstered by Plan México investments in Durango, Coahuila, and Sonora TIF facilities, the shift is capturing greater value-added processing inside Mexico. records.content: The Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) has confirmed bird flu is to blame for the deaths of dozens of birds at Monroe's Lake Tye Park. According to officials, it is now just a matter of waiting for the disease to run its course. In the meantime, warning signs have been posted all over the park, urging people to stay away from the birds. Last week, KIRO 7 paid a visit to Lake Tye Park and witnessed a bird likely suffering from the infection. It struggled to stand, stumbling around in circles before taking flight and crashing into a building. "It is disturbing to watch," said Staci Lehman, communications manager at WDFW. "It's tough to see any animal, whether wild or domestic, suffer like that." More than 30 birds were found in a matter of days last week. WDFW was called in to test some of the carcasses, which confirmed they had bird flu. WDFW said it has not recorded the total number of deaths in and around the park. Lehman said WDFW is tracking cases around the state, but Monroe saw the biggest cluster yet. "At this point, that is the biggest number we have seen," she said. It's not just in the wild. The Tacoma-Pierce County Health Department reported a poultry facility was put under quarantine after bird flu was found there. It said employees are being monitored for illness and disease control measures are being taken. Lehman said the most important step people can take is not to handle any wild birds, living or dead. Those who must are urged to wear protective equipment, double bag the carcass, and put it deep in their trash can so no scavengers can eat it. "We understand some people really want to help, so they think, 'Hey, I can nurse this bird back to health' or something like that," Lehman said. "That's why we ask you to call the department and let the professionals deal with it." The state department of health reports three cases in humans so far this year, one of which was fatal.
